noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: describe the composition of the blood: red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma
understand the role of plasma in the transport of carbon dioxide, digested food, urea, hormones and heat energy
understand how adaptations of red blood cells make them suitable for the transport of oxygen, including shape, the absence of a nucleus and the presence of haemoglobin

primer.text: Blood looks like one red liquid but is really a suspension: cells and fragments riding a straw-coloured carrier. Plasma hauls the dissolved cargo, red cells grab the oxygen, white cells fight, platelets patch. This note assigns each component its job and its shape.

lessons.title: The Four Components of Blood
lessons.opening: Blood suspends red cells, white cells and platelets in plasma, which fills over half the volume, with red cells claiming most of the remainder and the white cells and platelets sharing the small rest.
keyPoints: Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid carrying everything.
Red cells are biconcave discs without a nucleus, packed with haemoglobin.
White cells are large, nucleated defensive cells.
Plasma occupies over half of the blood's volume.

low.restatement: Plasma carries; red cells ferry oxygen; white cells defend; platelets patch holes.
low.analogy: A river barge: the river (plasma), the cargo crews (red cells), the guards (white cells) and the repair dinghies (platelets).
low.examPointer: Reproduce the table's structure column if asked to 'describe the composition'.

medium.restatement: Each component's structure anticipates its function: no nucleus buys haemoglobin space, a large nucleus runs defence chemistry, fragment status lets platelets jam into any gap.
medium.analogy: A well-cut crew uniform: every shape exists because of the job it must do.
medium.examPointer: Volume proportions get asked: over half plasma, most of the rest red cells.

check.stem: Which component makes up over half of blood's volume?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Red cells claim most of the remaining half.
White cells are a small fraction.
Platelets are the smallest share.

check.stem: Which structural feature do red blood cells lack?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Every cell keeps its membrane.
Haemoglobin is precisely what they contain.
That is the shape they have.

check.stem: Which component consists of cell fragments?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
They are whole, if unusual, cells.
Plasma is the fluid, not a fragment.
Those are whole white cells.

check.stem: How are white blood cells described in the composition table?

options.text: Large cells containing a large nucleus, with differing types and functions
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
That is the red cell description.
That describes plasma.
That describes platelets.

check.stem: What colour and form is plasma?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Red comes from the cells, not the carrier.
Plasma is liquid.
It is an aqueous solution, not oil.

check.stem: List the four components of blood.
check.modelAnswer: Red cells, white cells, platelets, and the plasma that carries them.

check.stem: Describe the structure of a red blood cell.
check.modelAnswer: A biconcave disc with no nucleus, containing haemoglobin.

check.stem: Explain why blood is described as a suspension rather than a simple solution.
check.modelAnswer: Because whole cells and fragments are held dispersed in the plasma liquid, rather than dissolved into it as solutes would be.

check.stem: A centrifuge spins a sample and separates layers. Predict the arrangement.
check.modelAnswer: Dense red cells pack at the bottom, white cells and platelets form a thin middle layer, and straw-coloured plasma sits on top.

lessons.title: Plasma, the Cargo Liquid
lessons.opening: Plasma transports the dissolved and suspended cargo of the blood: carbon dioxide from the cells to the lungs, digested food and ions from the gut, urea toward the kidneys, hormones to their targets, and heat toward the skin.
keyPoints: Carbon dioxide rides dissolved in plasma toward the lungs.
Digested food and mineral ions travel from the small intestine.
Urea is delivered to the kidneys for removal.
Hormones reach their target organs through the plasma.
Heat energy moves to cooler parts or to the skin for loss.

low.restatement: Plasma carries gas, food, ions, urea, hormones and heat around the body.
low.analogy: A delivery van's cargo bay: everything loose rides in the same compartment.
low.examPointer: Learn the five cargoes by name; one missing item costs the mark.

medium.restatement: Every listed cargo travels dissolved or suspended in the aqueous plasma, which is why the blood can service respiration, excretion, coordination and temperature control simultaneously.
medium.analogy: One river serving every factory along its banks.
medium.examPointer: Pair each cargo with its destination: lungs, cells, kidneys, targets, skin.

check.stem: Where does plasma take carbon dioxide?

options.text: From the respiring cells to the lungs
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: From the lungs to the cells
options.explanation: The flow of carbon dioxide runs the other way.
Urea goes to the kidneys; carbon dioxide goes to the lungs.
Carbon dioxide is not stored anywhere.

check.stem: Which plasma cargo heads for the kidneys?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Oxygen goes to respiring cells.
Hormones head for their target tissues.
Food heads for the cells that need it.

check.stem: What are hormones in the plasma?

options.text: Chemical messengers released by glands and delivered to target organs
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Waste products bound for the lungs
options.explanation: Hormones are signals, not wastes.
Digestion products are food cargo.
That is haemoglobin's role in the red cells.

check.stem: How does plasma help control body temperature?

options.text: It carries heat energy to cooler regions or to the skin where it can be lost
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Cooling comes from heat transfer, not freezing.
It redistributes heat rather than blocking it.
Generation happens in respiration; plasma only transports.

check.stem: Which cargo is absorbed from the small intestine into the plasma?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Urea is collected after liver action, not from the gut's absorption.
Carbon dioxide loads at the cells.
Antibodies come from lymphocytes, not digestion.

check.stem: List the five cargoes plasma transports.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, digested food, mineral ions, urea, hormones and heat energy.

check.stem: State where digested food is loaded into the plasma.
check.modelAnswer: Dissolved particles are absorbed from the small intestine.

check.stem: Explain why plasma's watery nature suits its transport role.
check.modelAnswer: Because water dissolves ions, sugars, urea and carbon dioxide readily, so one carrier liquid can serve every organ without switching vehicles.

check.stem: After a protein-rich meal, name the plasma cargo that rises and its destination.
check.modelAnswer: Digested food rises — amino acids absorbed from the small intestine — travelling to cells that need material for growth and repair.

lessons.title: Red Cells Built for Oxygen
lessons.opening: Red blood cells are oxygen ferries whose three adaptations work together: haemoglobin binds the gas, the absent nucleus frees space for it, and the biconcave disc shape enlarges the surface for rapid exchange.
keyPoints: Haemoglobin binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin.
No nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin.
The biconcave disc shape raises the surface-area-to-volume ratio.
Oxygen diffuses in and out quickly because of that shape.
Their cargo reaches every respiring cell in the body.

low.restatement: Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, no nucleus and a dimpled disc shape.
low.analogy: A van with every seat stripped out except the cargo racks.
low.examPointer: Name all three adaptations together when a question asks 'how are they adapted'.

medium.restatement: The three traits are a package: binding chemistry, packing space and exchange geometry each raise the oxygen delivery rate.
medium.analogy: A courier with the right satchel, a light frame and a short driveway.
medium.examPointer: If asked for the shape's advantage, quote the surface-area-to-volume ratio wording.

check.stem: What does haemoglobin do in a red blood cell?

options.text: It binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That is phagocyte work.
Clotting uses fibrin, not haemoglobin.
Urea rides the plasma.

check.stem: Why is the absence of a nucleus an advantage for a red cell?

options.text: It leaves more space to pack in haemoglobin
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It lets the cell divide faster
options.explanation: Red cells do not divide.

options.text: It makes the cell lighter to float
options.explanation: Buoyancy is irrelevant.

options.text: It allows oxygen through the membrane
options.explanation: Diffusion happens at the membrane regardless.

check.stem: What shape is a red blood cell?

options.text: A biconcave disc, dented inward toward its middle
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
No square shapes exist in blood.
That resembles a vessel, not a cell.
The dimple is the defining feature.

check.stem: What advantage does the biconcave shape give?

options.text: A larger surface-area-to-volume ratio for fast oxygen diffusion
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Shape is not armour here.
There is no nucleus.
Speed comes from blood flow, not cell shape.

check.stem: To which cells do red blood cells deliver their cargo?

options.text: Every respiring cell in the body
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The lungs load the oxygen; delivery is body-wide.
The brain is one customer among all.
Muscles are heavy users, not the only users.

check.stem: Name the oxygen-binding protein in red blood cells.
State the three adaptations of red blood cells.
check.modelAnswer: Packed haemoglobin, no nucleus, and a biconcave disc shape.

check.stem: Explain why the three red-cell adaptations function as a set.
check.modelAnswer: Because haemoglobin provides the binding chemistry, the missing nucleus provides the packing space for it, and the biconcave shape speeds the gas across the membrane — delivery depends on all three.

check.stem: At altitude, the body makes more red cells. Explain the benefit using their adaptations.
check.modelAnswer: More red cells means more total haemoglobin per litre, so the thinner-air oxygen still gets bound and delivered despite the lower partial pressure.

glossary.definition: The straw-coloured liquid suspending the blood's cells and carrying its dissolved cargo.
The red-cell protein that binds oxygen into oxyhaemoglobin.
Dented on both faces, the red-cell shape that enlarges its surface.
The nitrogen waste carried in plasma to the kidneys.
